items.title: Measuring the state of open science in transportation using large language models
items.abstract: Open science initiatives have strengthened scientific integrity and accelerated research progress across many fields, but the state of their practice within transportation research remains under-investigated. Key features of open science, defined here as data and code availability, are difficult to extract due to the inherent complexity of the field. Previous work has either been limited to small-scale studies due to the labor-intensive nature of manual analysis or has relied on large-scale bibliometric approaches that sacrifice contextual richness. This paper introduces an automatic and scalable feature-extraction pipeline that combines full-text extraction and human agreement analysis in order to measure code and data availability in transportation research. We employ Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task and validate their performance against a manually curated dataset and through an inter-rater agreement analysis. We applied this pipeline to examine 10,724 research articles published in the Transportation Research Part series of journals between 2019 and 2024. Our analysis found that only 5% of quantitative papers shared a code repository, 4% of quantitative papers shared a data repository, and about 3% of papers shared both, with trends differing across journals, topics, and geographic regions. We found no significant difference in citation counts or review duration between papers that provided data and code and those that did not, suggesting a misalignment between open science efforts and traditional academic metrics. Consequently, encouraging these practices will likely require structural interventions from journals and funding agencies to supplement the lack of direct author incentives. The pipeline developed in this study can be readily scaled to other journals, representing a critical step toward the automated measurement and monitoring of open science practices in transportation research. An interactive explorer can be found on the project page https://www.rerite.org/MOST .

items.title: Mechanism‐Guided and Data‐Driven Design of COF/MOF Photocatalysts Toward H 2 O 2 Production
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) is a green oxidant and potential energy carrier, and the photosynthesis of H 2 O 2 from water and oxygen offers a sustainable alternative to the conventional anthraquinone process. Due to the tunable skeletons, adjustable pore microenvironments, and designable active sites, covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and metal‐organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as crystalline porous photocatalysts for H 2 O 2 production. This review summarizes recent advances in COF/MOF photocatalysts for H 2 O 2 production, focusing on density functional theory (DFT)‐based mechanistic insights, descriptor construction, and data‐driven catalyst discovery enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). We first discuss how DFT calculations elucidate active sites, charge‐transfer pathways, and reaction mechanisms by revealing electronic structures, excited‐state charge distributions, adsorption behavior, and reaction free‐energy profiles. We then highlight how DFT‐derived descriptors can bridge mechanistic understanding with materials screening. Finally, we discuss how AI and ML approaches integrate experimental performance, reaction conditions, structural features, and theoretical descriptors to enable candidate screening and design‐rule extraction. Overall, the integration of DFT calculations with AI/ML methods provides a promising route toward mechanism‐guided and data‐driven discovery of COF/MOF photocatalysts for solar‐driven H 2 O 2 production.

items.title: Medical AI: are Osler's principles lost in translation?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform clinical practice, but its adoption coincides with a longstanding decline in bedside medicine. Herein, we argue that reintroducing Oslerian principles into medical training may be essential to ensure that technological progress does not come at the expense of the physician-patient relationship. Throughout, we use the term AI to refer to tools built on algorithms, from risk calculators and predictive models to large language models, that produce predictions, classifications or recommendations. These tools have no agency of their own: they operate only on the data supplied to them, and their implementation depends on how clinicians and institutions design and deploy them.William Osler never saw an algorithm. He died in 1919, a century before "artificial intelligence" entered the clinical vocabulary. And yet no figure in the history of medicine is better equipped to tell us what we are about to lose 1 . Osler's central achievement was a discipline of the mind: the conviction that the practice of medicine must rest on direct observation of the patient and on the relationship between patient and physician. We argue that this discipline is now under direct threat, and that AI tools, as currently deployed, tend to hasten its erosion rather than reverse it -unless we act deliberately to stop it. In fact, the physician-patient relationship has already been reshaped by decades of patient access to medical information through the internet and social media. This shift has been amplified by the development of health-related AI tools, which increase patients' knowledge but also expose them to misinformation and misinterpretation. Nowadays, patients often arrive at the clinical encounter having already formed their own interpretations about their disease, which directly impacts the dialogue with the physician from the very first minutes of the encounter -a dynamic Osler never had to confront. Oslerian principles must therefore be adapted to this new reality, in which both physician and patient increasingly approach the clinical encounter already shaped by algorithms.Clarifying what AI can do -and will not do in the foreseeable future AI tools can go extraordinarily far in the medical process -synthesizing literature at a scale no human can match, flagging patterns in imaging and pathology that trained eyes miss, drafting notes, triaging risk, generating differential diagnoses, and suggesting therapeutic options in seconds. None of this is in serious dispute anymore, and clinicians who dismiss it outright are being unrealistic.On the other hand, it is illusory to imagine that AI will, in the foreseeable future, replace clinical observation and the personal relationship between doctor and patient. This needs to be said plainly, not hedged. Diagnosis by patternmatching on data is not the same as sitting at the bedside of anxious patients, watching how they behave, picking up on what they leave unsaid, and actually building the trust that makes adherence possible. Whatever level of performance AI models will achieve in the future, they will remain trained on the past, and no model can substitute for what happens, uniquely, in the present, between two people.There is also a more technical reason why bedside medicine remains indispensable: AI can only reason about the reality that has been captured and digitized. An algorithm implicitly assumes that what is absent from the record does not exist. Because important information reaches the record only if a physician observes it, an algorithm working from an incomplete record can return a seemingly precise but inaccurate output, creating an illusion of certainty. Oslerian observation is therefore not a nostalgic complement to AI but a technical prerequisite for its validity: no AI tool can compensate for a hurried or incomplete examination. Far from making clinical skills obsolete, AI demands sharper skills in listening, observation and physical examination.Losing the lessons learned at the bedside is not a hypothetical risk, nor is it a new one. For decades, medical departments have been organized around organ systems and specialized technologies. This process of specialization and subspecialization -a transformation that long predates the current wave of AI adoption -has produced remarkable diagnostic and therapeutic advances, but it has also fragmented the physician's view of the patient as a whole and made a holistic approach harder to sustain. Another powerful driver of this change has been the growth of administrative and documentation burden: in ambulatory practice, a time-and-motion study found that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct clinical face time with patients 2 , and administrative burden has been associated with lower intrinsic motivation among physicians and poorer patient-reported experience of care 3 .Consistent with this, studies among internal medicine trainees have documented a clear decline in direct time with patients for well over a decade 4 , and the trend is still underway today in several disciplines. For example, in hematologic malignancies, where AI-based tools are being rapidly adopted to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions 5 , physicians increasingly spend more time in offices in front of computer screens -reviewing algorithmic outputs, multiomic profiles, and risk calculators -often making therapeutic decisions before they examine the patient, so that the consultation risks becoming a confirmation of a decision already made elsewhere, rather than the encounter from which the decision should emerge. Deployed carelessly, AI tools are likely to deepen this pattern rather than correct it. Many current incentives push in that direction: institutions will reward the efficiency of deciding early, physicians will gravitate toward the workflow that is faster and less cognitively taxing, and the tools themselves are easiest to deploy on data that are already structured and available before the visit. Left to market and workflow pressures alone, AI is unlikely to restore the clinical encounter and may further hollow it out. This is the central danger. However, AI can also work in the opposite direction. In a recent randomized trial, ambient AI scribes, which transcribe the consultation and draft the clinical note, were associated with reduced physician burnout, and doctors reported that the technology allowed them to engage better with their patients 6 . Such tools can return the physician's attention from the screen to the patientprovided that the time they free is deliberately protected for the clinical encounter.This is precisely why Osler's teaching should not be treated as an outdated precept, but as the specific countermeasure this moment requires. We argue that it should be urgently reintroduced as a structural component of clinical education, integrated into, not appended to, the technical curriculum. Three Oslerian principles should anchor that effort: "Listen to the patient; he is telling you the diagnosis." What the physician personally learns at the patient's bedside should always come first -a principle physicians in subspecialty training are especially at risk of losing, as AI output can easily become the main input they consult before reaching a conclusion. AI output should inform that conclusion but not replace it."Medicine is learned by the bedside and not in the classroom." Osler's most consequential reform was moving medical education out of the lecture hall and to the patient's side. A century later, the direction of travel has reversed: trainees now often learn to interpret data before they learn to examine a patient. That sequence needs to be corrected, with protected, unhurried bedside time built into training and explicitly shielded from the pressure to consult the algorithm first. "Imperturbability." In his famous 1889 address, Aequanimitas 7 , Osler used this word to describe the calm and steady judgment a physician needs when facing suffering, urgency and clinical uncertainty. Applied to the output of AI, the same discipline must hold: neither adopting it blindly, a failure known as automation bias 8 , nor dismissing it out of hand, but checking it as rigorously as any other clinical evidence, including against what the physician has personally observed.These principles cannot be reintroduced as a simple return to an earlier era; they must be adapted to a clinical environment now shaped not only by AI but also by electronic health records, an ever-expanding volume of diagnostic data, and patients arriving informed -and sometimes misinformed. The task for training programs is not to teach learners to resist these developments but to integrate them without displacing direct observation and reasoning. Concretely, this could include bedside practice that requires trainees to form their own clinical impression before consulting AI output, case studies comparing bedside findings with AI-generated information, exercises showing how omissions in the history or examination alter an algorithm's output, and communication exercises on discussing AI- derived information with patients. These skills should be embedded into formal assessment and not treated as incidental.Discussions on "AI and the future of medicine" too often lead to wishful thinking that is very unlikely to be implemented. Instead, they should lead to concrete proposals, such as treating the clinical encounter as a parameter to be measured in academic medical centers. Time at the bedside is a necessary but insufficient indicator, since more time does not automatically translate into better care. We therefore propose mixed metrics combining the time physicians actually spend with patients, the diagnostic accuracy of the physician working with AI compared with either alone, and patients' perceptions of empathy and trust assessed with validated instruments such as the Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) measure 9 .William Osler would have welcomed the advent of AI in medicine, but he would have insisted that every AI tool be held to a single non-negotiable question: does it bring the physician closer to the patient, or does it interpose itself between them? On present evidence, in disciplines already reorganized around screens and algorithms, many AI deployments are failing that test 10 . The remedy is not to slow the technology down. It is to speed up, urgently, the reintroduction of Osler's principles into the training of every physician who will use it.

items.title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use
items.abstract: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.

items.title: Metacognitive Scaffolds Create Productive Friction for AI-Assisted Knowledge Work
items.abstract: Generative AI imposes new metacognitive demands on knowledge workers as their work shifts from production to planning, evaluation, and orchestration. In a randomized, between-subjects experiment on AI-assisted writing (297 workers, 594 essays), we test dynamically-generated metacognitive scaffolds supporting goal specification and task decomposition. We find that scaffolds improve writing quality, with this boost persisting in short-lag transfer when scaffolds are removed. We also find evidence of improved topic recall three days later. These effects are consistent with observed changes in how people learn to prompt AI systems after exposure to scaffolding. However, scaffolded participants rate the AI as less helpful and more cognitively demanding even as they perform better, suggesting that subjective ease can understate the value of support. Our findings make the case for metacognitive scaffolds in AI-assisted knowledge work, revealing a productive friction worth designing for as workers increasingly delegate work to agentic AI.

items.title: Metaheuristic Optimization and Artificial Intelligence in Wind Energy Systems for Sustainable Environment: Forecasting, Control, Design, and Diagnostics—A Critical Review
items.abstract: Wind power is the largest renewable energy source used at the sustainable utility scale. However, wind turbine design, siting, forecasting, control, and maintenance face real challenges, mainly because wind speed is variable and poorly predictable. Over the last ten years, researchers have applied both artificial intelligence (AI) models and metaheuristic optimization algorithms across all phases of the wind energy value chain. This review examines these two methodological approaches across four application fields, with particular attention to evaluation practice, validation level, and implications for sustainability. First, we review wind speed and power forecasting, from statistical baselines to machine learning and deep learning architectures, including models that rely on metaheuristics to tune their hyperparameters and decomposition stages. Second, we examine control applications, focusing on metaheuristic tuning of generator and converter controllers (mainly rotor-side control of doubly-fed induction generators), pitch and torque control, and maximum power point tracking (MPPT). Third, we discuss design-level optimization, covering blade aerodynamic design and wind farm layout under wake effects. Fourth, we examine machine-learning-based supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) monitoring and fault diagnosis, including normal-behavior modelling and anomaly detection. Finally, as floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) are a cross-cutting emerging field, with coupled hydro-aero-elastic problems in control co-design and AI-based monitoring, the paper proposes a research agenda for the next sustainable generation of onshore and offshore wind systems, focused on standardized open benchmarks, uncertainty-aware forecasting, physics-informed learning, and hardware-validated optimization.

items.title: Między wsparciem a zagrożeniem: koncepcje potoczne osób studiujących pedagogikę wczesnoszkolną i przedszkolną wobec generatywnej sztucznej inteligencji w edukacji
items.abstract: The aim of the article is to reconstruct the lay conceptions held by students of early childhood and pre-primary education regarding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and its potential role in education. The study is grounded in the constructivist-interpretive paradigm, adopting an understanding of learning as a process of active construction and negotiation of meanings. The empirical material was collected using a questionnaire consisting of open, exploratory questions. The participants were students who had already completed coursework related to didactics but had not yet taken courses on modern technologies. A non-probability purposive sampling strategy was applied. The collected data were analyzed using interpretative thematic analysis. The results reveal tension in students’ common understandings of GenAI. On the one hand, GenAI is perceived as a tool that increases teacher effectiveness and facilitates access to information. On the other hand, the same feature raises concerns about limiting students’ cognitive independence. The results further suggest that future teachers’ ways of thinking about GenAI may be closely related to their understanding of the nature of learning and educational culture. Therefore, the study highlights the need to incorporate reflection on GenAI into teacher education – not as a technical issue, but as a didactic one.

items.title: Mitigating Saliency Collapse: Robust Saliency-Aware Long-Text Image-Text Alignment
items.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA

items.title: Motivation across Academic Performance Groups among First-year Undergraduate Physiotherapy Students in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India: A Cross-sectional Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Physiotherapy education in India is transitioning to a competency-based curriculum that emphasises selfdirected learning. Academic motivation is a key learner-related factor that influences academic outcomes. However, evidence on motivational profiles across academic performance groups remains limited, especially among physiotherapy students. Understanding these differences may facilitate targeted educational support to improve academic outcomes. Aim: To assess academic motivation and compare advanced, average, and Slow Performers (SLP) among undergraduate physiotherapy students. Materials and Methods: The present multicentre crosssectional study was conducted from March 2025 to December 2025 in private physiotherapy colleges affiliated with Maharashtra University of Health Sciences located in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. A complete enumerative sampling technique was used to recruit 509 eligible first-year physiotherapy undergraduates. Students who took the first formative exam were included. Based on exam scores, students were classified as advanced (top 20%), average (middle 60%), or SLPs (bottom 20%). Data were collected using the Academic Motivation Scale via Google Forms and Analysed applying the Mann-Whitney U test and Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction (p<0.017). A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: A total of 450 participants were included for the final analysis, comprising 74 males (16.44%) and 376 females (83.56%). Significant differences were observed among the three academic performance groups for intrinsic motivation to know (H=13.25, p=0.001) and amotivation (H=13.97, p=0.001). Post-hoc analysis showed significant differences in intrinsic motivation to know between advanced and SLPs, and between average and SLPs, while amotivation differed significantly between advanced and SLPs. Conclusion: The findings of the present study demonstrate that advanced performers exhibited higher intrinsic and lower amotivation than SLPs, although the differences were small. Moreover, extrinsic motivation types did not differ. Integrating early assessment of academic motivation and autonomysupportive learning environments may help reduce amotivation and enhance learner engagement.

items.title: Multi-Tool Selection for Robotic Systems: Comparing Semantic Retrieval and LLM
items.abstract: Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request. This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools. We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods - fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval - and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline. The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools. Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822, compared with 0.8869 for the large-model baseline. Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity. These results identify a quality-latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.

items.title: Nanotech and AI in Vertical Farming: A Technological Revolution
items.abstract: With the worldwide vertical farming market expected to reach US$33.02 billion by 2030, rising at a compound annual growth rate of 25.1% from 2022 to 2030, vertical farming is becoming increasingly important as a key solution to handle food insecurity, urbanization, and climate change. This chapter investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) and nanotechnology might improve vertical farming systems. By means of technologies including nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, and nanosensors, which improve nutrient delivery efficiency by 20–30% and hence lower agrochemical waste by up to 50%, nanotechnology enables precision agriculture. AI algorithms, through machine learning and computer vision, enable real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and automated decision making simultaneously, so increasing crop yields by up to 35% and lowering resource consumption (water, electricity, and labor). Integration of nanoscale materials with AI-driven analytics helps to create intelligent farming ecosystems, therefore optimizing environmental controls and enhancing food quality in small urban environments. The synergistic possibilities of these technologies, current developments, implementation difficulties, and their combined influence on the direction of smart agriculture and urban food sustainability are covered in this chapter.

items.title: Negotiating English Language Teaching in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Constructivist Grounded Theory of Secondary School Teachers’ Pedagogical Adaptation in Philippine Public Schools
items.abstract: This qualitative study examined how secondary school English teachers in Philippine public schools negotiate and reconstruct pedagogy in response to artificial intelligence (AI). Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, the study drew on intensive semi-structured interviews with seven English teachers from selected public secondary schools under the Schools Division Office of Batangas City. Initial and focused coding, constant comparison, memo writing, and theoretical integration generated seven interrelated categories: continually recalibrating pedagogical practice; protecting the learning work from technological substitution; reconstructing assessment to make learning and authorship visible; negotiating ethical boundaries through contextual professional judgment; building adaptive capacity through collegial and institutional support; cultivating critical AI literacy while preserving human voice and communication; and mediating AI access to preserve equity and inclusive participation. Findings indicate that responsible adaptation involves recursive, context-sensitive professional judgment. Teachers evaluated whether AI supported intended competencies, preserved valid assessment and authorship, maintained ethical safeguards, and enabled equitable participation. The categories informed the emergent AI-Responsive English Pedagogy Framework. The study concludes that responsible integration requires bounded technological augmentation, professional learning, flexible institutional guidance, assessment redesign, and protection of authentic language learning.

items.title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

items.title: Network-level control of G protein-coupled receptors: a panacea for chronic diseases?
items.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) modulate diverse hormonal, metabolic, neural, and immunological signaling processes. Their age-dependent decline accounts for many fundamental hallmarks of aging, including low-grade inflammation (inflammaging), mitochondrial failure and energy dysregulation, genomic instability and epigenetic dysregulation, dysregulated cellular communication, loss of proteostasis, and cellular senescence. Consequently, GPCR dysfunction underpins nearly all chronic, age-related diseases, including cardiovascular disease, cancer, various endocrine disorders, and neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases. Therefore, the GPCR network (“GPCR-ome”) constitutes a central, druggable, “mega-trophic” regulator of human healthspan. Individual GPCRs present numerous therapeutic targets for specific conditions, many of which are already being exploited, while others show future promise. Alongside this disease-centric approach, the GPCR-ome offers the more radical opportunity to rebalance entire signaling networks to simultaneously correct the multisystem pathological effects of aging itself. Here, we outline a transformative paradigm for network-level, GPCR-based geroprotection that employs artificial intelligence, digital twins, and quantum computational methods to design biased agonists, allosteric or multitarget modulators, heteromer-selective ligands, and polypharmacological strategies to mitigate and manage age-related disorders. We also explore how combinatorial GPCR-based strategies (e.g., coupled with senolytic, metabolic, or regenerative medicines) hold compelling promise to delay multiple hallmarks of aging and enable personalized anti-aging GPCR therapies based on multiomic biomarkers.

items.title: Neuroforge Interactive Learning V1
items.abstract: This working paper presents Neuroforge Interactive Learning V1, a reproducible pilot study of rule identification through binary success/failure feedback. The experiment evaluates a symbolic learning agent against a fixed, non-learning baseline across 100 seeded episodes, with 16 actions per episode (1,600 actions per policy). The fixed baseline achieved 25.50% action accuracy (408/1,600), while the feedback-learning agent achieved 91.94% (1,471/1,600). All four automated tests passed in the local evaluation. The learner identifies an active rule from four predefined candidates using feedback. Its memory resets between episodes. The experiment does not establish neural-network learning, general artificial intelligence, autonomous discovery of arbitrary rules, or transfer to previously unseen rule families. The paper documents the experimental setup, observed results, limitations, and proposed future work toward interactive rule discovery and cross-task generalization. This is an independently authored, non-peer-reviewed research working paper associated with QuantEdge AI LLC.

items.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
items.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. items.title: NNJA—a curated archive of Earth system observations from 1970s to present for reanalysis and data-driven model development
items.abstract: Abstract The NOAA-NASA Joint Archive (NNJA pronounced like the word ninja) is a publicly accessible, curated collection of Earth system observations spanning 1979 to present, created to accelerate reanalysis production, support development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, and enable access to the observational record underlying modern reanalyses. The archive encompasses atmospheric satellite radiances and conventional measurements, in-situ ocean profiles, sea ice concentrations and freeboard retrievals, and land surface observations from over 60 sensors provided by NOAA, NASA, and their partners. The number of atmospheric records increases from around 10 6 observations per day in 1979 to around 10 8 in the modern era. The dataset extends into near-real time through continuous archival of the NOAA operational data. NNJA observations are distributed through Amazon Web Services in formats compatible with established data assimilation systems and are accompanied by channel-level black and white lists that capture the quality history of the satellite record. Data integrity is verified through a three-tier process: file-level metadata checks, cross-validation against existing black and white lists from prior NOAA and NASA reanalyses, and a comparison of assimilation statistics with reference reanalysis and operational products. To lower barriers for the machine learning community, a companion dataset (NNJA-AI) transforms NNJA observations from legacy formats to column-oriented Apache Parquet, enabling sufficient large-scale queries and direct integration with AI training workflows. This article describes the creation, verification, and curation of the NNJA dataset, document its current scope and known limitations, and discusses its role as a shared observational infrastructure for the next generation of U.S. reanalyses.

items.title: Numerical Analysis Applications in Improving Engineering Models
items.abstract: Numerical analysis serves as the fundamental pillar of modern engineering modeling, providing the mathematical and computational tools necessary to transform complex physical equations into practical numerical solutions. This study reviews contemporary applications of numerical analysis in enhancing engineering models, focusing on methodological advancements in solving partial differential equations, data-driven model order reduction techniques, adaptive mesh methods, and machine learning-based surrogate models. The study employs a synthetic analytical approach that combines a review of recent literature with an analysis of empirical results from various numerical methods, addressing hybrid models that integrate traditional techniques with artificial intelligence. The analysis demonstrates that combining traditional numerical analysis methods with artificial intelligence and reduced-order models has revolutionized the ability of engineers to simulate complex multiphysics systems with unprecedented accuracy and computational efficiency; hybrid models have achieved computational speedups ranging from 72 to 522 times compare to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study addresses challenges related to computational cost and solution sensitivity to initial conditions, examining cutting-edge innovative solutions such as physicsinformed neural networks and causality-based learning. The study concludes that future trends in this field are shifting towards the development of hybrid models that combine analytical accuracy with computational speed, with an increasing emphasis on generalization capabilities beyond the training data. This opens up broad prospects for digital engineering and digital twin applications across the industrial, energy, and infrastructure sectors. The study offers a comprehensive perspective on the development of engineering models using advanced numerical analysis techniques and identifies promising future research directions in this vital field.

items.title: Occupational risk profiles among public officials in Korea: A survey-based application of a first-tier risk assessment tool
items.abstract: Public officials perform diverse administrative, public-facing, emergency, and safety–critical tasks, yet their occupational risk profiles have rarely been characterized across actual job functions. In Korea, public officials have historically remained partly outside core occupational safety and health requirements, and systematic evidence on their occupational risk profiles across diverse job functions has been limited. This study applied the Public Officials’ Occupational Risk Assessment (PORA) tool to 36,779 Korean public officials to screen perceived occupational risks and identify occupation- and job-function-specific high-risk patterns. Respondents assessed exposure frequency and intensity for 24 occupational risk factors across psychological, organizational, ergonomic, physical, chemical, and biological domains. Risk scores were calculated as the product of frequency and intensity, and high-risk responses were defined as “high” or “very high” according to the PORA risk matrix. Prolonged sitting showed the highest mean risk score and high-risk prevalence, followed by public-facing work, fast work pace, time pressure, emotional stress, awkward posture, and repetitive upper-limb work. Frequency–intensity comparisons showed that some risks were driven by frequent exposure, whereas event-based psychological hazards received lower time-proportion-based frequency ratings but relatively higher intensity ratings. Occupation-specific logistic regression showed distinct profiles: general service officials were characterized by prolonged sitting and time pressure, police officers by broad psychological, ergonomic, and physical hazards, and firefighters by physical, chemical, biological, and emergency-response-related hazards. Job-function heatmaps and hierarchical clustering further revealed heterogeneous risk profiles across 22 main job functions. These findings highlight the need for job-function-based, participatory, and risk-prioritized occupational safety and health management in public organizations.

items.title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their use as the backbone of foundation recommendation models (FRMs). Existing methods enhance recommendations through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning under a Think-then-Answer paradigm. However, explicit CoT incurs substantial inference overhead by generating lengthy reasoning traces and relies on manually designed templates that struggle to capture diverse, dynamic user interests. We propose OneLatent, an efficient latent reasoning framework that compresses explicit reasoning traces into several learnable latent tokens, enabling Latent-Reason-then-Answer inference without generating verbose traces. OneLatent first introduces Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT), which creates diverse, high-quality teacher-generated supervision by exploring user interests from multiple perspectives and automatically adapting reasoning complexity to each instance. Building on pretrained FRMs, it then uses a three-stage latent-token alignment paradigm to progressively internalize CoT traces into learnable latent tokens. Finally, a multistage curriculum-based post-training strategy activates latent-token reasoning for downstream recommendation tasks. Experiments on an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark show that OneLatent consistently outperforms explicit CoT-based methods and traditional baselines. Compared with the Think and No-Think variants of FRMs, OneLatent improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, while achieving over 17x higher online inference throughput. We further develop a production serving system for scalable, real-time FRM inference. An online A/B test in Kuaishou's local-services advertising scenario shows that deploying OneLatent with this system yields an estimated 9.6% revenue lift over strong online baselines, including OneRec and OneReason.

items.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics
items.abstract: Abstract Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

items.title: Optical and Photonic Computing for Deep Learning Acceleration: Silicon Photonics, Mach-Zehnder Meshes, and Wavelength-Division Multiplexing
items.abstract: The relentless exponential scaling of foundation models and transformer architectures has pushed conventional silicon complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) digital accelerators (GPUs, TPUs) toward fundamental thermodynamic and interconnect boundaries. Joule heating, resistance-capacitance (RC) interconnect delay scaling, and the 'memory wall' severely constrain energy efficiency and compute density. Optical Computing and Integrated Silicon Photonics (SiPh) establish an analog non-Von Neumann hardware paradigm that executes fundamental linear algebra operations—specifically General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication (GEMM)—at the speed of light with near-zero runtime energy dissipation. By encoding vector-matrix activations into coherent optical wave fields and modulating light through cascaded Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI) meshes, Micro-Ring Resonator (MRR) banks, and Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM) waveguides, photonic tensor processing units (PTPUs) execute analog matrix multiplications in continuous time with sub-nanosecond propagation latencies. However, translating integrated photonic circuits into production deep learning accelerators introduces profound optoelectronic engineering bottlenecks: analog noise accumulation across deep optical meshes, severe thermal phase drift, limited electro-optic Digital-to-Analog / Analog-to-Digital (DAC/ADC) conversion resolution, non-linear activation implementation hurdles, and wafer-scale optical footprint scaling. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of integrated photonic computing for deep neural network acceleration. We formalize the Clements and Reck unitary matrix decomposition algorithms over reconfigurable MZI topologies, derive the optical transmission transfer matrix under optical carrier phase error perturbations, and establish energy-per-MAC physical thermodynamic bounds across electro-optic conversion interfaces. Furthermore, we construct an empirical co-simulation and hardware testbed benchmarking silicon photonic meshes against state-of-the-art CMOS accelerators (NVIDIA H100, Google TPU v5p) across vision transformers, large language model attention heads, and resonant graph convolutions. Our empirical findings demonstrate that a 64x64 integrated MZI photonic mesh achieves a 58.4x improvement in energy-delay product (EDP) over 4nm digital CMOS cores, sustaining up to 128 Tera-Operations per Second per Watt (TOPS/W) at 4-bit to 8-bit equivalent precision, while active thermo-optic phase stabilization preserves 98.2% baseline classification accuracy. Finally, we establish open research directions in all-optical non-linear activation functions, co-packaged optical memory architectures, and wafer-scale photonic interconnect scaling.

items.title: Optimization of Water Supply in Smart Cities: An Integrated Approach to Data Management, Artificial Intelligence, and Smart Water Technologies
items.abstract: Amid growing water scarcity and losses in distribution networks, it is crucial to find effective solutions that increase efficiency and ensure the sustainability of water management. This global demand is reflected in the regional scenario of the state of Bahia, especially in the capital, Salvador. Data from the Bahia State Basic Sanitation Regulatory Agency (AGERSA) points to recurring problems with water interruptions that are not sufficiently unpredictable. Based on this issue, this article presents a literature review on emerging technologies to improve water supply management in smart cities, with specific application to the capital of Bahia. The methodology employed involves a technical review of the main technologies currently applied in Smart Water Networks, including smart meters and advanced sensors for water quality monitoring, proposing an integrated model based on the Internet of Things (IoT) and Big Data analysis (AI; Machine Learning).The expected results include improved operational efficiency, greater accuracy in early detection and response to critical events such as leaks and supply interruptions, as well as greater transparency of water supply and treatment information for users and managers. The conclusion is that the implementation of the solution will significantly contribute to the technical, operational, and environmental sustainability of urban water systems.

items.title: Organisational support for evidence-based practice in occupational health services in Finland
items.abstract: There is very little published research about evidence-based practice (EBP) in occupational health services (OHS), and none to date in Finland. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) model of evidence-based healthcare provides a clear and intuitive conceptual framework for exploring how research evidence and the practice of medicine could be better integrated. Thus far it has seen very little use within the occupational health arena. This study explores the extent of organisational support given to OHS professionals in providing EBP in Finland. We collected survey data ( n = 524) from Finnish OHS physicians and nurses involved either solely in patient care duties or also in a managerial, development or expert role, using a validated online questionnaire (EBP-OHS) that was made available in two waves: in November 2020 and August 2021. We analysed quantitative data using descriptive methods and qualitative data using content analysis. Most respondents reported that their organisations value evidence-based practice (83%) and encourage staff to use evidence-based information (74%). In their opinion, the most important means to support EBP were managerial support and example, employee training, and a dedicated team or expert responsible for ensuring that care delivery consistently aligns with the latest evidence. The respondents wanted clear and uniform processes for implementing research evidence into practice, and IT systems that support both the implementation and reporting of EBP in practice. Successful EBP in OHS seems likely to require managers to set a good example, both in their attitude and actions. Building a culture of implementing EBP requires staff to be empowered to share and keep up with robust and relevant new evidence and to be allocated sufficient time to do so. OHS units need to have clear structures and forums dedicated to engaging in EBP. OHS would likely benefit from having clear implementation processes and EBP tools that allow systematic follow-up and reporting.

items.title: Organized and self-organized football activity and motivational regulation among boys and girls in a Norwegian youth talent pathway: A descriptive cross-sectional study
items.abstract: In talent pathways that formally include both sexes, it remains unclear whether boys and girls selected into the same pathway accumulate comparable football activity. This study aimed to (1) describe sex-stratified self-reported weekly football exposure and motivational regulation among 103 players (51 girls, 52 boys; 13.8 ± 0.9 years) selected for one regional division of a Norwegian national youth talent development program, and (2) describe age-cohort patterns across the ≤13-, 14- and 15-year cohorts. Players reported weekly football hours and sessions during the preparation period and competitive season. Because the dataset lacked club- and training-group identifiers, observations could not be assumed independent; the study is therefore descriptive and exploratory: sex-stratified exposure and motivational regulation are summarized as median [interquartile range, IQR], age-cohort exposure as mean ± SD, and between-sex patterns as differences in central tendency rather than as hypothesis tests. In this sample, boys reported higher total weekly football exposure than girls (median 10.8 vs. 7.0 h), with a proportionally larger difference for self-organized than organized activity. Boys reported slightly higher intrinsic motivation and identified regulation, whereas girls reported slightly higher amotivation, external regulation and introjected regulation; these differences were small relative to the scale range, and both groups reported high intrinsic motivation and low amotivation in absolute terms. Because players were drawn from shared but unmodeled development environments in a cross-sectional design, the findings are descriptive only: equal formal selection did not coincide with equal football exposure, particularly in self-organized activity, generating hypotheses for future cluster-aware studies.

items.title: PAIR: Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval for Premium People Recommendation at LinkedIn
items.abstract: General-purpose embeddings trained on profile similarity often misrank candidates in professional networks, where relevance is inherently complementary rather than symmetric. For example, job seekers usually engage with recruiters rather than peers with similar credentials. Current user recommendation systems are often built on profile similarity or social signals such as shared connections, which are effective in friend-oriented social networks where users tend to connect with similar people or within existing social circles. However, this does not hold in professional platforms like LinkedIn, where interactions are often goal-driven and cross-role interactions, requiring matching based on complementary intents rather than similarity or social proximity. In this paper, we propose Preference-Aligned Intent Retrieval, a retrieval framework that is designed to model user intent preference instead of profile similarity. Our approach is inspired by the preference-learning perspective of Direct Preference Optimization, but instantiates preference learning as an exposure-conditioned multi-negative contrastive objective over embeddings. This formulation simplifies training and scales efficiently to large candidate sets without requiring an explicit reference model. Furthermore, we incorporate user interaction history by aggregating click histories with positional encoding to capture temporal order, which enables constant-cost updates of user representations over a fixed history window, allowing new interactions to be incorporated without re-encoding history. As a result, personalization can be updated efficiently using lightweight CPU operations without repeated LLM inference during serving. We evaluate PAIR on LinkedIn's Premium retrieval task. A 0.6B parameter model achieves a MAR@100 of 0.45.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models to a Low-Resource Agglutinative Language: A Corpus, Datasets, and a Reproducible Benchmark for the Bashkir Language
items.abstract: Bashkir is a low-resource agglutinative language written in Cyrillic and remains poorly represented in modern LLMs. We present an open resource suite and a systematic benchmark of adaptation methods: the Bashkir Web Corpus (71,567 documents, 46.9M tokens, 16 sources) and three labelled datasets for binary, multiclass and multilabel text classification; the benchmark covers the first two. Experiments use eight architectures (82M-8B: DistilGPT2, GPT-2 base/medium, Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B, YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B, mBERT, XLM-R) and three adaptation groups (full fine-tuning, QLoRA, in-context learning), plus continual pretraining (CPT). (1) QLoRA on 3.8-8B models outperforms encoder-only fine-tuning on binary classification: YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B with CPT reaches macro-F1 0.748 vs 0.653 (XLM-R) and 0.650 (mBERT); pairwise differences are significant after Holm correction (p<0.001). (2) YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B significantly outperforms Mistral-7B and Phi-3-mini on multiclass classification, BPB and native-speaker ratings (mean 3.28 vs 2.52 and 2.22; n=100; alpha=0.69-0.77; p<0.05); on binary classification its QLoRA advantage is not significant (p>=0.084). (3) CPT effects depend on model and task: perplexity improves for Phi-3-mini (+0.58) and YandexGPT-5-Lite-8B (+0.33) but worsens for Mistral-7B (-1.15, p<0.001); on binary classification CPT helps Mistral-7B most (+4.0 macro-F1). (4) Tokeniser fertility on Bashkir varies 2.67x (2.92-7.80) and tracks adaptation quality, while perplexity across tokenisers is not comparable. Cyrillic tokenisers with Russian pretraining are preferable; LLM judges reproduce native ratings for grammar and coherence (rho=0.33-0.46) but not language correctness (rho=0.16, p=0.11); native evaluation remains necessary. All artefacts are open-licensed.

items.title: Passing the Wrong Test: Model Size and Discriminant Validity in LLM-Based Psychological Assessment
items.abstract: Validation studies of zero-shot language-model scoring of psychological interviews often rely primarily on a single convergent correlation with a questionnaire to establish validity. However, a bivariate correlation cannot reveal whether a model lacks discriminant validity, agrees poorly in absolute terms, produces non-random missing scores, or scores inconsistently. We evaluated eight open-weight families (1–70B active parameters) and eight commercial frontier models. The models scored the same sets of clinical interviews (Study 1: suicide recovery, n = 149; Study 2: future self-continuity, n = 164) across 52 configurations. Convergent validity improves with model size in both studies. However, the standard open-weight models tested achieve only about three-quarters of frontier convergent validity, with 11-fold greater mean absolute bias, more format failures, and lower repeatability in Study 1. In Study 2, standard open models (≤ 27B) are as strongly correlated with a closely related construct (suicide recovery) as with the target (mean difference −0.014), although they correlate less strongly with a distal neighbor (life satisfaction). All six frontier generations correlate more strongly with the target than with either neighbor (mean difference from recovery +0.117). On a local workstation, Gemma 4 31B is within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, outperforming its similar-sized predecessor. Llama 3.3 70B shows no greater discriminant validity than Gemma 4 31B, suggesting that discriminant validity is a function of release, not parameter count alone. Based on these findings, we suggest a minimum validation standard across five domains.

items.title: Patch Management or Public Law? A Critical Comment on the Five Eyes Guidance for the Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
items.abstract: On 1 May 2026, six Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies jointly issued Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services, the first coordinated Anglophone statement on the governance of LLM-based autonomous agents. This Comment argues that, although the Guidance offers competent cybersecurity risk management within its stated remit, its institutional weight invites a broader governance reading that the document cannot bear, and that five structural limitations then come into view. First, the cybersecurity doctrines on which it relies are necessary but insufficient for agentic systems, whose delegated authority, underspecified goals, and long-horizon autonomy strain the assumptions of conventional controls. Second, it privatises systemic risk by imposing duties on deployers without specifying public-law obligations, redress, or liability across the agentic value chain. Third, it prescribes human oversight without specifying the conditions of effective control, so that responsibility risks being assigned to reviewers who lack the information, authority, or time to exercise it. Fourth, it reduces accountability to auditability, confusing a technical property with a legal relation between duty-holders and affected parties. Fifth, the security-defined mandates of its six authoring agencies, and the intelligence-oversight structures within which most of them sit, raise questions of institutional voice, while its Five Eyes-only authorship raises a risk of divergence from the AI frameworks now emerging in the European Union, the Republic of Korea and Japan. The Comment concludes by outlining the elements of an enforceable, rights-protective, cross-jurisdictional legal regime that should supplement, rather than be displaced by, the technical controls the Guidance recommends.

items.title: Patient Perception and Trust in Artificial Intelligence in Dental Care: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Background: Patient trust may determine whether artificial intelligence (AI) is accepted in dental care, particularly when AI contributes to diagnosis or treatment planning. We aimed to synthesize patient-reported trust, confidence, acceptance, and preferences regarding dental AI and to identify factors associated with these outcomes. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 2 June 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed with the revised JBI tool for analytical cross-sectional studies. Because outcomes and metrics were heterogeneous, findings were synthesized narratively. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261439049). Results: The final synthesis included eight studies comprising 3171 participants from five countries. Attitudes were generally favourable when AI supported rather than replaced dentists. In one study, 47.7% accepted AI-assisted interpretation of diagnostic data, whereas 10.8% trusted an entirely AI-generated diagnosis. Another study found that 84.9% supported AI analysis of dental images followed by dentist review. A fixed-order vignette study improved lesion recognition but did not significantly change trust in the dentist. Interpretation was limited by non-probability sampling, heterogeneous and often non-validated measures, incomplete control of confounding, and reporting inconsistencies. Conclusions: Available evidence suggests conditional acceptance of dental AI, particularly when dentists retain oversight. Confidence in the prevalence estimates of trust and acceptance is low; these findings do not establish that AI improves trust. More representative studies using validated, conceptually distinct outcome measures are required.

items.title: Pedagogical Practices and Reflections on AI-Enhanced Innovation in Sustainability Education: Guiding AI Integration Through the IDEA Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing sustainability education by providing dynamic tools that foster systems thinking, data literacy, ethical reasoning, and creative problem solving. Yet despite growing experimentation with AI in teaching and learning, there remains a notable gap in practice-based frameworks that guide educators in integrating AI into ESD in ethically grounded and pedagogically purposeful ways. Addressing this need, this chapter explores how AI can be thoughtfully integrated into Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) through innovative pedagogical approaches. Drawing on teaching cases and reflective analysis, it introduces the IDEA (Innovation, Design, Evaluation, and Anchoring) framework as a structured yet flexible guide for integrating AI into practice. The framework is illustrated through practice-informed vignettes, including the use of generative AI for futures thinking, machine learning for environmental data analysis, AI-powered feedback in ethics debates, and co-designed projects with pre-service teachers. These examples highlight both the affordances and tensions of using AI in higher education and teacher preparation programs. The IDEA framework encourages educators to critically examine how AI tools align with sustainability goals, support meaningful learning outcomes, and surface issues of ethics, equity, and digital competence. Situating AI not as a disruptive novelty but as a pedagogical mediator, the chapter contributes to the discourse on ESD and the responsible integration of emerging technologies. Drawing on interdisciplinary scholarship, it reflects on implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and education policy, offering actionable recommendations for creating ethical, inclusive, and future-facing learning environments.

items.title: PENERAPAN GAMIFIKASI BERBASIS PROYEK UNTUK MENINGKATKAN MOTIVASI BELAJAR MURID SMP
items.abstract: This study was initiated by the uneven learning motivation among junior high school students in Coding and Artificial Intelligence (CAI) subjects. The research aims to enhance students’ learning motivation through a project-based gamification strategy. The method employed was Classroom Action Research (CAR) based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, conducted in two cycles with 31 students as subjects. The learning process implemented Project-Based Learning (PjBL) integrated with six gamification elements (clear goals, points, challenges, badges, feedback, and leaderboards) through a simple Scratch game development project. Data were collected using an adapted Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), observations, field notes, and documentation, and analyzed descriptively. The results showed an increase in students’ learning motivation, with the classical average rising from 3.06 (76.39%) in the pre-cycle to 3.24 (81.00%) in Cycle I and 3.38 (84.39%) in Cycle II, and all motivation aspects improving. Students reaching the minimum “High” criterion (score ≥ 3.00) increased from 51.61% (16 students) in the pre-cycle to 77.42% (24 students) in Cycle I, and reached the classical success target at 80.65% (25 students) in Cycle II. In Cycle II, a layered troubleshooting strategy using a Generative AI chatbot as a coding assistant, followed by peer feedback, appeared to support more persistent and independent problem-solving, although the gains were moderate and uneven across students, and self-regulation remained the lowest-scoring aspect (3.09). In conclusion, project-based gamification was accompanied by an increase in junior high school students’ learning motivation in CAI subjects.

items.title: PENERAPAN MODEL PEMBELAJARAN DISCOVERY LEARNING BERBANTUAN ARTIFICAL INTELLIGENCE TERHADAP HASIL BELAJAR PESERTA DIDIK KELAS X PADA MATERI TEORI ASAM BASA
items.abstract: Penelitian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh penerapan model pembelajarn Discovery Learning yang belum terlaksana secara optimal, serta penggunaan Artificial Intelligence dalam pembelajaran yang masih bersifat umum, belum terarah, dan belum dimanfaatkan secara inovatif sebagai pendukung proses belajar peserta didik. Kondisi tersebut menyebabkan peserta didik masih mengalami kesulitan dalam memahami konsep-konsep kimia yang bersifat abstrak. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui pengaruh penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan Artificial Intelligence terhadap hasil belajar peserta didik pada materi teori asam basa. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode pre-experimental design dan desain One Group Pretest-Posttest Design. Sampel penelitian terdiri atas 35 peserta didik kelas X.E di SMK SMAK Makassar yang dipilih menggunakan teknik purposive sampling. Teknik pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui tes hasil belajar berupa pretest dan posttest. Analisis data dilakukan menggunakan statistik deskriptif dan inferensial melalui uji prasyarat yakni uji normalitas, dilanjutkan uji hipotesis nonparametric yakni Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, dan analisis N-gain. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan Artificial Intelligence memberikan pengaruh terhadap peningkatan hasil belajar peserta didik. Nilai N-gain berada pada kategori tinggi sehingga model pembelajaran tersebut efektif dalam meningkatkan hasil belajar peserta didik pada materi teori asam basa.

items.title: Performance of Naïve Spectral Geometric Models in Histopathology AI
items.abstract: Abstract Spectral geometric methods provide mathematically interpretable representations of tissue morphology, yet their standalone performance in histopathology artificial intelligence has not been systematically evaluated. This study benchmarks purely spectral pipelines across representative digital pathology and spatial omics tasks relative to convolutional baselines. Spectral features derived from graph Laplacians, heat kernel signatures, spectral wavelet energy, Slepian concentrations, fractal descriptors, and persistent homology were extracted from histopathology patches using fixed-grid graphs. Features were processed using spectral neural operators and gradient boosting. Four tasks were evaluated: binary breast cancer classification (BreaKHis), multi-class glioblastoma region-patch classification, spatial transcriptomics prediction (10× Visium), and spot-wise denoising. Cross-validation and leave-one-slide-out strategies were applied. Metrics included accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), mean squared error, and Pearson correlation. Equivalence between spectral and CNN models was not established within the prespecified ±0.03 AUC margin. Purely spectral models achieved lower performance than convolutional baselines, with AUC differences of 0.12–0.23. The CNN→LGBM model achieved an accuracy of 0.83 ± 0.06, balanced accuracy of 0.73 ± 0.10, and AUC of 0.80 ± 0.13. Equivalence was not established within the prespecified margin. Fusion achieved balanced accuracy of 0.73 ± 0.08, equal to the CNN baseline mean balanced accuracy, without surpassing CNN AUC. Spatial transcriptomics prediction showed limited cross-slide generalization (Pearson correlation 0.06), whereas spot-wise denoising under sparse conditions showed competitive performance. Spectral geometric models do not outperform convolutional methods for classification or segmentation but provide complementary utility in denoising and sparse spatial settings.

items.title: Physical and Mental Health Consequences of Work-Related Stress: A Comparative Study of Women and Men
items.abstract: Work-related stress is a leading occupational health concern, and a substantial literature suggests its consequences differ between women and men. Most of that literature, however, establishes that a difference exists without identifying the mechanism responsible. This study examined the physical and mental health consequences of work-related stress among employed women and men, and tested whether differences persisted after psychosocial working conditions were controlled. A comparative cross-sectional design was adopted. Data were collected from 101 full-time employees aged 25-50 in Bengaluru, India; the analytical sample comprised 100 participants (50 women, 50 men). A 50-item instrument assessed perceived stress, working conditions, physical symptoms, emotional wellbeing and coping. Physical health and emotional wellbeing scales showed good reliability (alpha = .83 and .86). Five of six hypotheses were unsupported: women and men did not differ in perceived stress (p = .584, d = -0.11), physical symptoms (p = .986, d = 0.004) or emotional wellbeing (p = .575, d = 0.11), and gender did not moderate the stress-health relationship. One significant difference emerged: men reported greater problem-focused coping (p < .001, d = -0.73), although the predicted difference in emotion-focused coping did not appear. Perceived stress correlated strongly with physical symptoms (r = .55) and emotional wellbeing (r = .62), explaining 30% and 39% of variance. Findings are consistent with a differential-exposure account: where working conditions were comparable, health consequences were comparable.

items.title: PIU Smart Intelligence Agents: Design and Implementation of a Security-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture for Enterprise Intelligence
items.abstract: Enterprises increasingly rely on heterogeneous documents, relational databases, and analytical systems to support information retrieval and business decision-making. Integrating large language models (LLMs) with these sources introduces challenges in evidence reliability, analytical correctness, access control, and operational resilience. This paper presents PIU Smart Intelligence Agents, a security-aware multi-agent architecture designed to integrate enterprise document intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, document summarization, naturallanguage-to-SQL analytics, key performance indicator (KPI) generation, and conversational AI within a common application and governance framework. The proposed architecture organizes specialized AI capabilities around shared services for authentication, authorization, request validation, provider integration, observability, and controlled data access. Its document-processing workflow encompasses file validation, text extraction, optical character recognition for scanned documents, normalization, chunking, embedding generation, and vector-based indexing. The structured-analytics workflow separates schema-aware query generation from SQL validation, restricted database execution, and result interpretation. The architecture also addresses provider compatibility, timeout handling, failure recovery, document lifecycle management, and traceability of generated outputs. The source implementation reports 1,242 automated tests passed and two integration tests skipped. These results are reported implementation evidence and have not been independently reproduced. The available evidence does not establish comprehensive external RAG benchmark performance, quantitative correctness across all agents, independently validated security effectiveness, or production-scale performance and recovery guarantees. Accordingly, this study presents an integrated engineering architecture and identifies a reproducible evaluation framework for assessing its effectiveness. The principal contribution is the systematic integration of heterogeneous enterprise AI capabilities with explicit governance and validation requirements, rather than the introduction of a new learning or retrieval algorithm. Future work should prioritize agent-specific correctness testing, retrieval and answer-quality benchmarks, adversarial security evaluation, controlled load testing, and recovery verification.

items.title: Pixels to precision: Deep learning in dental imaging
items.abstract: Dental imaging is fundamental to diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up in Oral Medicine and Maxillofacial Radiology. Although conventional radiographic interpretation remains dependent on professional expertise, diagnostic performance may be influenced by observer variability, image quality, workload, and the subtle nature of early pathological changes. The development of Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), has introduced new approaches for automated analysis of dental and maxillofacial images. This narrative review discusses the evolution, principles, applications, clinical relevance, limitations, and future directions of deep learning in dental imaging, with emphasis on intraoral radiography, panoramic radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and related imaging modalities. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated applications in dental caries detection, periodontal bone assessment, periapical lesion detection, tooth identification and numbering, jaw lesion analysis, anatomical segmentation, and treatment planning. More advanced architectures, including U-Net, residual networks, object-detection models, three-dimensional CNNs, and emerging transformer-based systems, have expanded the scope of automated image interpretation. However, the rapid growth of research has also highlighted important limitations, including small and heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent annotation, retrospective study designs, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, and difficulties in explaining model predictions. Importantly, high algorithmic accuracy does not necessarily translate into clinical effectiveness. Future research should therefore focus on diverse multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, explainable AI, multimodal systems, ethical governance, and meaningful human-AI collaboration. Deep learning is most appropriately viewed as an adjunctive clinical decision-support technology that complements rather than replaces professional diagnostic judgment.

items.title: PlaceIntel: A Multi-Agentic AI-Powered Campus Placement Management and Preparation Platform
items.abstract: Abstract— Preparing students for campus recruitment in a personalized and effective way is still difficult for most colleges. Typical placement systems deal mainly with administrative work such as registering students, storing company details, checking eligibility, and organizing recruitment drives, whereas interview training and companyspecific preparation are usually left to separate resources. This paper describes PlaceIntel, a web platform driven by multiple cooperating AI agents that unites central placement administration with tailored AI support for students. Four dedicated agents form the core of the system: a Mock Interview Agent, a Company Preparation Agent, a Company Research Agent, and a Skill Gap Analyzer. A Candidate Evaluation module additionally supports structured assessment during placement drives. The implementation relies on React, Java Spring Boot, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, LangGraph, and Gemini 3.6 Flash; authentication is handled with Spring Security and JWT, while Docker and AWS are used for deployment. The resulting architecture brings placement operations and AI-guided preparationtogether within a single modular design.
